csvschema

Self-describing CSV files with embedded, loss-tolerant schemas.

csvschema writes and reads CSV files that carry their own schema inside ordinary data columns, so the file opens as a plain CSV in every tool and the schema survives sorting, filtering, row loss, encoding changes, and spreadsheet round-trips. The name is the joke: the file looks schemaless and is not.

It does four things:

  1. Packetize a table schema (field names, types, formats, missing codes, factor levels, keys) into short ASCII tokens and spread redundant copies through one or more _schema columns.
  2. Recover the schema from any surviving subset of rows, verify it, and apply it (types, factors, NA codes) on read.
  3. Canary the data: store a purposeful sample of fragile values per variable in a _canary column and report, after a round-trip, whether each variable is still intact and, if not, how it was damaged.
  4. Point to an optional Frictionless datapackage.json sidecar and cross-check hashes in both directions.

The schema is encoded the way the internet survives a hostile channel: every packet is one unquoted, pure-ASCII token ({{S1/8~ein^str^uniq^req~c41d9a02}}) with its own index, total, and CRC-32, plus a whole-schema hash, spread redundantly so it survives heavy row loss.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lecy/csvschema")

Quick start 

library(csvschema)

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")

# Write a self-describing CSV (dg_states ships with the package).
cs_write(dg_states, path)
#> csvschema: 18 packets, c=6, p=5; survives random loss of 80% of rows ...
# (50 rows need more copies to survive 80% loss; a 2,000-row table needs c=1, p=1.)

# The file is a perfectly ordinary CSV with two extra character columns.
# Read it back: the schema is recovered and applied automatically.
out <- cs_read_csv(path)
#> csvschema: schema verified (inband); 16/16 variables intact

str(out[, c("region", "south", "motto_year")])
#> 'data.frame':  50 obs. of  3 variables:
#>  $ region    : Factor w/ 4 levels "Northeast","South",..
#>  $ south     : logi  TRUE FALSE FALSE TRUE ...
#>  $ motto_year: int  1923 1967 1863 1907 ...

region comes back as the original factor, south as logical, motto_year as integer — none of which a plain read.csv() would restore.

Surviving damage

The schema survives losing most of the rows, because each packet is repeated and striped across the file:

few <- read.csv(path)[sample(50, 10), ]          # keep 10 of 50 rows
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv"); write.csv(few, tmp, row.names = FALSE)
cs_read_csv(tmp)
#> csvschema: schema verified (inband); ...

The cs_corrupt_*() family simulates every vector in the threat model, so you can test your own pipeline:

out <- cs_read_csv(path)
rep <- cs_report(out)       # the recovery + canary report
rep$status                  # "verified"
rep$canary                  # per-variable: verdict and named damage

How much redundancy? 

cs_copies(20, f = 0.2)                 # 76 copies to survive 80% row loss
cs_redundancy(20, 2000, f = 0.2)$sentence
#> "survives random loss of 80% of rows with failure probability ..."

What it does not do

  • Delete every _schema column and the in-band schema is gone; use the sidecar (cs_write(..., sidecar = TRUE)), which is independent.
  • Case-folding every cell (some mainframe/SQL loaders) is detected, not recovered: the per-packet CRC covers the exact-case payload, so folded payloads fail their check and are dropped. Recovery reports the loss rather than returning a silently wrong schema.
  • Numeric precision and NA vs "": doubles are written at R’s default precision, and with the default missingValues = [""] an empty cell reads back as NA.
  • Erasure coding, non-CSV containers, and encryption are out of scope for v0.1.

Compatibility

A fixture is round-tripped through common CSV tools and the recovery and data-damage results recorded in inst/compat/. Every scriptable tool tested so far — base R, readr, data.table, arrow, vroom, and line-based row subsets — recovers the schema (verified); the canary names what each one did to the data (the zero-padded 9-digit ID and the 17-digit ID are the usual casualties, read as an integer and a double). Other tools (Python, DuckDB, SQLite, spreadsheets, …) are listed there as not yet tested.

Specification

The wire format is specified normatively, and independently of R, in inst/specs/wire-format.md — complete enough to write a conforming reader or writer in another language.

Relationship to Frictionless

The canonical schema model is Frictionless Table Schema v2. csvschema adds a wire encoding, not a new schema language: cs_schema_to_frictionless() and cs_schema_from_frictionless() convert losslessly for the supported subset, and the sidecar is a standard Data Package.
